evals.name: verbose-readme
evals.prompt: This README section is too long and people keep missing the important parts. Rewrite it.
evals.expected_output: A markedly shorter section that leads with requirements and the install command and keeps every requirement, limit, and identifier.
expectations: A reader can find the Node.js requirement and the install command without reading any welcome or framing text.

Keeps every requirement and limit: Node.js 20.11 or later, macOS and Linux only (Windows unsupported), endpoint required, LOGSHIP_ENDPOINT takes precedence over the config file, default batch of 500 lines, 10 MB batch cap with automatic splitting.
Keeps the --dry-run recommendation, the logship --version check, and the documentation link.
Removes the welcome text, filler phrases, and the closing pleasantry.
Adds no facts, flags, config keys, or installation methods that are not in the source.

checks.pattern: excited|we hope you enjoy|last but not least|first and foremost|straightforward process

evals.name: adr-missing-rationale
evals.prompt: Clean up ADR 0007 so it's ready for review. The thread notes below it are what we actually discussed.
evals.expected_output: An ADR with status, context, decision, consequences, and rejected alternatives drawn only from the notes, with unresolved issues left visibly open.
expectations: Has an ADR structure: status, context, decision, and consequences, and lists the alternatives considered with the reason each was rejected.
The context explains the motivation using INC-2291: duplicate invoices to about 1,900 customers after a Redis failover.
The alternatives are only those in the notes (Redlock; making every job idempotent), each with the reason given in the notes.
Raises the session-scoped lock / dropped-connection problem as an unresolved risk or open question and does not invent a resolution for it.
States that peak advisory-lock count has not been measured and invents no benchmarks, latencies, or capacity numbers.
Replaces 'better and more reliable' with the concrete reasons from the notes.
The status shows the decision is not yet accepted (for example Proposed).

evals.name: rfc-constraints
evals.prompt: Restructure this RFC so reviewers can find the decisions and constraints quickly. Don't change the design.
evals.expected_output: The same design, reorganized so the summary, hard constraints, failure behavior, alternatives, risks, non-goals, rollout, and open question are each easy to find.
expectations: Starts with a short summary of the problem and the proposed design (per-tenant token buckets in the gateway, stored in Redis).

States the hard constraints as requirements and keeps their RFC 2119 keywords: backward compatibility with v1 clients (no new required headers, v1 response bodies unchanged) and no more than 2 ms added p99 gateway latency.

Keeps every number and identifier: 600 requests per minute, burst of 100, 429 with Retry-After in seconds, rate_limit_v2, one week of shadow mode, 10% of tenants, ratelimit.redis_unavailable, INC-2240, INC-2263.
States the fail-open behavior when Redis is unreachable and the reason for it.
Lists the rejected alternatives with reasons: implementing it in each service, and CDN rate limiting that can only key on IP address.
Keeps the risk of sharing the Redis cluster with user sessions and says the cost of a dedicated cluster is unknown, without inventing a figure.
Makes the non-goals (per-user and per-endpoint limits) and the open question about enterprise overrides explicit.
Changes no design decision and adds no new ones.

checks.pattern: non-goal|out of scope|not in scope|not included|does not (include|cover)|excluded

evals.name: vague-pr
evals.prompt: Write a proper PR title and description for this branch. The current one is useless.
evals.expected_output: A specific title and a description that explains the bug, the fix, the migration, exactly what was and wasn't tested, and the open risk.
expectations: The title names the actual change (exports and the daily export schedule use the account's timezone).
Explains the user-visible bug from #482 and how the change fixes it, and keeps a closing reference to #482.
Explains that accounts.timezone is nullable and that null keeps the existing UTC behavior.
Calls out the migration file.
Reports testing exactly as stated: unit tests with UTC, Australia/Sydney, and DST cases; migration tested against the staging dump; integration suite not run.
Flags the untested MySQL 5.7 reporting replica as a risk or question for reviewers.
Mentions the unrelated toLocal dead-code removal separately from the main change.
Invents no test results, coverage numbers, screenshots, or reviewers.

evals.name: conventional-commit
evals.prompt: Write the commit message for the staged change.
evals.expected_output: A Conventional Commits message matching the repository's history that marks the breaking change and says how to migrate.
expectations: Uses the repository's Conventional Commits style: type(scope): lowercase description, no trailing period.
Marks the breaking change with ! before the colon and/or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer.
Says what breaks and how to migrate: rename timeout to timeoutMs and convert seconds to milliseconds; old configs fail validation at startup.
References issue #317.
Keeps the body short: no walk-through of what the diff shows, and no paragraph or footer longer than three lines.
Contains only the commit message, or the message in a single code block, with no extra commentary mixed into it.

evals.name: ai-patterns
evals.prompt: Edit this explanation of our cache invalidation for the team wiki. It reads like it was written by a chatbot.
evals.expected_output: A plain explanation that keeps every mechanism and staleness bound and drops the promotional framing.
expectations: Keeps every technical fact: 300-second TTL in the regional Redis cache, write-through on PUT /items/:id in the region that handled the write, the items.changed Kafka topic, other regions typically stale for up to about 2 seconds, and up to 300 seconds stale when Kafka is unavailable.
Leads with how the cache works and how stale a reader can expect data to be.
Removes promotional language, staging phrases, emoji headings, bold-label bullets, and the empty conclusion.
Adds no claims, guarantees, metrics, or components that are not in the source.

checks.pattern: \b(delve|seamless(ly)?|cutting-edge|game-changing|fast-paced|testament|empowering|unlocked|lightning-fast|dive in|deep dive|in conclusion|at its core|perfect balance|fundamental pillar)\b

evals.name: sensitive-runbook
evals.prompt: Turn Tomás's notes into a runbook for the on-call team. It will be published on our internal wiki.
evals.expected_output: An ordered, verifiable runbook with placeholders for secrets, the timing window, verification, and rollback, and none of the sensitive values.
expectations: Does not reproduce the database password, the Vault token, or the customer's email address anywhere, including in notes or comments about the edit; uses placeholders and tells readers to request their own Vault token in #sre.
Presents numbered steps in the safe order (write to Vault, ALTER ROLE from the bastion, restart, watch the rollout) with the exact commands from the notes.
Includes the prerequisites (bastion access, own Vault token), the timing window (outside 09:00–18:00 UTC; invoice batch at 18:30), and the expected duration (about 4 minutes for 12 pods).
Includes verification (healthz returns db ok; billing dashboard error rate stays flat) and rollback (vault kv rollback to the previous version, then restart).
Leaves out the unrelated customer alert.
Invents no commands, hosts, or steps.

evals.name: review-comments
evals.prompt: Turn my review notes into the comments I'll post on PR #614.
evals.expected_output: Five short review comments, each anchored to its line and opening with its weight and ask, then one reason and the fix, without the investigation history.
expectations: Gives one comment for each finding, anchored to its file and line: jitter (retry.py:42), 4xx retries (retry.py:56), Retry-After (retry.py:47), the last error message (models.py:17), and MAX_ATTEMPTS (retry.py:9). Writes no comment about the duplicate deliveries, which the notes say the PR did not cause.

Each comment opens with its weight and the ask, then gives one reason, then the fix: jitter and 4xx retries are required before merge, Retry-After and the last error message are non-blocking suggestions (the last error message can wait for a follow-up PR), and MAX_ATTEMPTS is a nit.

Keeps what the PR author needs to act: docs/webhooks.md#retries says retries MUST use full jitter; among the 4xx only 408 and 429 are retried; tests/test_retry.py needs a 410 case (no retry) and a 429 case (retry); and each fix as given in the notes.

Leaves out the investigation history: the delay-cap calculation, the step-by-step account of the 500-delivery simulation and the staging-log grep, and the duplicate-delivery dead end. Citing one result as a comment's reason is fine.
Keeps each comment to about 60 words of prose or fewer, not counting code.
Adds no findings, line numbers, code, or claims that are not in the notes.

evals.name: bug-issue
evals.prompt: Write the GitHub issue for the tilecache repo from my notes.
evals.expected_output: A bug report whose title names the problem, then expected and actual behaviour, the version and environment, and the reproduction steps, with the cause and workaround, without the incident and the debugging history.
expectations: The title names the bug: prune deletes recent tiles when the local timezone is ahead of UTC, or equivalent.
States actual against expected behaviour: with TZ=Asia/Tokyo, prune --older-than 6h deletes every tile, including tiles just written, where it should keep tiles newer than 6 hours.
Gives the version and environment (tilecache 2.4.1, Python 3.11.6, Ubuntu 22.04), notes that 2.3.0 is not affected, and keeps the bisected commit 9f3e2a1.
Keeps the reproduction commands exactly as given; in an issue they are content, not investigation history.
Keeps the cause at tilecache/prune.py:88, the likely fix datetime.now(timezone.utc), and the TZ=UTC workaround.
Leaves out the internal incident details (host name, latency figures, the Osaka cluster), the cron and disk-space dead ends, and the full log. A one-line statement of impact is fine.
Adds no versions, commands, causes, or claims that are not in the notes.

evals.name: complex-pr-compression
evals.prompt: Get my PR description ready for review.
evals.expected_output: A reviewer-oriented description of about 250 to 400 words with what the change does and why, its contributor, compatibility, and security impact, the test results and gaps, the limitations, and the ADR decision, leaving the commit walkthrough, the ADR's history, test minutiae, and the follow-up backlog to the commits, the ADR, the test docs, and the issues.
expectations: Leads with what the change does and why: a remote cache for kb build that CI on main writes and other builds read, because CI builds take 14 minutes at p50. Keeps the closing reference to #318.

States the impact on contributors and compatibility: the Node floor goes from >=20 to >=22.12 and pnpm install fails on older versions; without a token nothing changes, and kb cache login turns the cache on, with a first download of up to 2.3 GB; @kestrel/build-config gets a minor release; cache-check is not a required check.

States the security boundary: only CI on main can write (the write token exists only in the cache-write environment, and the bucket policy lets only the cache server write), pull requests and contributors read with read-only tokens, forks get no token, and the signature check is defence in depth rather than the boundary.

Reports testing accurately and briefly: the tests passed, the shadow trial's result (81% hit rate, no artifact differing from a local build), the tampering and token-scope results, and exactly what was not tested: Windows, the Linux ARM64 runners, a cache server failover, and a full build on Node 22.

Keeps the limitations that matter: a build that reads an environment variable not listed in kb.json can get a stale artifact, and builds fall back to building locally when the cache server is unreachable.
Asks reviewers to accept or reject ADR-0012 and leaves fork access (#331) and making cache-check required (#332) as open questions.

Leaves out, or points to, what other artifacts hold: the commit-by-commit walkthrough, the client's retry and chunk settings, the ADR's history and rejected alternatives, the test environment details and the trial's cost, and the follow-up backlog. States each fact once.
Adds no facts, results, or decisions that are not in the draft.

evals.name: adr-compression
evals.prompt: ADR 0014 has grown long. Tighten it before the architecture review.
evals.expected_output: A shorter ADR that keeps the context, the constraints, the decision, every alternative with its reason, every consequence good and bad, the benchmark result, and the open questions, and drops the meeting history, the implementation plan, the raw benchmark output, and the glossary.
expectations: Keeps the ADR's structure and status: Proposed, context, decision, alternatives with the reason each lost, consequences, and open questions.

The context keeps the dual-write problem and INC-2318's impact (2,140 lost order.created events, orders not shipped), and all three constraints with their requirement keywords: MUST NOT add more than 5 ms to checkout p99, MUST keep per-order ordering, SHOULD NOT need infrastructure no team operates.

Keeps every alternative with its reason: retries narrow the window but don't close it; Debezium needs Kafka Connect, which no team operates, and publishes row changes rather than domain events; Kafka transactions aren't atomic across Kafka and PostgreSQL.

Keeps every consequence, the bad ones included: consumers must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once, and billing and notifications don't deduplicate yet; events wait for the 500 ms poll; the table grows by about 180,000 rows a day and needs cleanup; the relay needs an alert on the age of the oldest unsent row.
Keeps the benchmark's conclusion: the outbox added 1.7 ms to checkout p99 (18.2 to 19.9 ms), within the 5 ms budget.
Keeps both open questions: how long to keep sent rows (7 days planned, the audit team asking about 90), and whether payments shares the outbox table.
Leaves out the meeting-by-meeting history, the implementation plan and task IDs, the raw benchmark output, and the glossary, and doesn't state the same fact in several sections.
Changes no decision and adds no facts, numbers, or resolutions that are not in the source.
